agricola-de-re-metallica-1912:
Georgius Agricola wrote De Re Metallica in Latin in 1556. Herbert Clark Hoover and Lou Henry Hoover gave it English dress in 1912. Hoover was a mine man long past when he took up the task. The book is the great text on mines and metal work of its age.

Twelve books tell of shafts, pumps, ores, and the smelt of each metal. Fine wood cuts show the craft at work, gear by gear. Agricola writes from years at the mines of Bohemia. The Hoover dress, with its rich notes, made the book a prize of the trade.
annales-cambriae-ingram-1912:
The Annales Cambriae, or Annals of Wales, are a Latin chronicle kept year by year in medieval Wales. James Ingram translated them into English in 1912. Most entries are bare lines about kings, battles, and deaths, the plain record of a small nation's memory.

Two short entries changed literary history. One notes Arthur's victory at Badon in 516, where he carried a cross into battle. Another records Camlann in 537, where Arthur and Medraut fell. From those stark lines grew centuries of argument about whether Arthur lived at all. The whole Arthurian tradition leans on this spare chronicle.
arxiv-2510-00112:
A. Comastri and a team of co-authors published this 2025 astronomy paper on black holes found by the James Webb Space Telescope. Many of these early active galaxies shine in infrared light yet vanish in X-rays. That X-ray weakness is a puzzle, since growing black holes usually glow in both. The team stacked deep Chandra telescope data to hunt for a faint shared signal.

They combined data on 50 type-1 and 38 type-2 active galaxies in two deep sky fields. For the type-2 group, a signal finally appeared in the hardest X-ray band. The pattern fits gas so thick that only the most piercing X-rays escape. The type-1 group stayed silent even after stacking, deepening the mystery around it. The work suggests at least some early black holes hide behind near-total blankets of gas.
arxiv-2510-00412:
Gwangyong Gwon wrote this 2025 mathematics paper proving that a natural question about polynomial maps has no algorithmic answer. Start a polynomial dynamical system at an integer point and iterate it forever. The orbit either runs on endlessly or eventually falls into a repeating loop. Gwon asks whether any program could always decide which fate a given system meets.

The proof starts from Turing machines and their eventual periodicity, itself shown undecidable here. That undecidability then transfers to orbit finiteness for systems on infinite tuples of integers. No algorithm can settle the question in general, however cleverly it is built. Results like this map the hard boundary between dynamics and computation theory. They warn that long-term prediction questions can be impossible in principle, not merely hard in practice. The paper is short, but its conclusion is absolute.
arxiv-2510-00512:
Yuanfang Xiang and Lun Ai published this 2025 paper on predicting how cells respond when genes are perturbed. Such predictions test our mechanistic grasp of the cell, yet data and curated knowledge often disagree. Noise, wrong labels, and gaps make naive integration brittle. Their framework, ALIGNED, fuses neural learning with symbolic knowledge under abductive learning.

The system aligns predictions against both the data and the knowledge base at once. A balanced consistency score grades that double agreement fairly. Knowledge itself gets refined systematically when the data keeps overruling it. In tests, ALIGNED beat leading methods on the balanced consistency measure. It also rediscovered biological relationships that experts recognize as meaningful. The authors argue the approach moves past black-box prediction toward transparent, evolving biological understanding. Future extensions could plug in protein interaction or metabolic networks as the knowledge side.
arxiv-2510-00612:
Jan Korbel, Remah Dahdoul, and Stefan Thurner published this 2025 paper modeling elections as a physics phase transition. Voters feel two forces: neighbors who think alike, and the pull of two rival campaigns. The setup maps exactly onto a classic random-field magnet model. The authors ask when campaign money tips the whole electorate into polarization.

Past a critical spending level for both parties, local influence stops mattering. Outcomes then mirror the campaigns' shares of aligned voters, regardless of the totals spent. A hysteresis band appears where incumbency, not spending, decides the result. Calibrated on United States House elections from nineteen eighty to twenty twenty, the threshold lands near one point eight million dollars. Races crossing that line surged in twenty eighteen and twenty twenty. The model reads recent polarization as a spending-driven regime change.
arxiv-2510-00712:
Mphako-Banda, Kriel, and Alochukwu introduce a new graph colouring parameter in this 2025 arXiv paper on discrete mathematics. Proper colourings forbid any edge joining two vertices of the same colour, and the chromatic number counts the fewest colours needed. Their k-defect number relaxes that rule in an edge-centred way: it is the smallest number of colours in a colouring with exactly k monochromatic edges, nicknamed bad edges. Setting k to zero recovers the chromatic number.

The authors establish basic properties of the parameter and derive bounds for trees, cycles, and wheels. They generalize several classical chromatic-number results to the framework. A curious feature emerges: for some graphs and positive k, no colouring achieves exactly k bad edges, however many colours are allowed. They map impossible ranges for bipartite and complete graphs, and they pose open questions on bounds for other graph families.
arxiv-2510-00912:
Hofmann and Tholen generalize Lawvere's notion of Cauchy completeness to normed categories in this 2025 arXiv paper on category theory, dedicated to Robert Paré. Lawvere's 1973 insight read metric spaces as categories enriched over the extended real half-line. Completeness of a metric space then became representability of adjoint distributors, which for ordinary categories is the idempotent-split property. Lawvere also sketched normed categories, enriched over normed sets, and the two threads were never joined.

The authors join them for any commutative quantale in place of the half-line. Their main theorem characterizes Lawvere completeness for categories enriched over normed sets over that quantale. They also improve recent results on normed convergence of Cauchy sequences in two major examples. Concrete corollaries show that categories of Lawvere metric spaces under natural norms are Cauchy cocomplete. The paper closes a conceptual gap that had stood since Lawvere's paper.
arxiv-2510-01112:
Desmond and Ramsey argue that astrophysics should move from correlation to causation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Galaxy studies usually link properties statistically, then test theories against those links. Correlations alone cannot say which properties drive which, in what direction, or whether hidden confounders fake a link. Causal discovery, a method common in genomics and epidemiology, is built to recover exactly that structure, yet astronomy barely uses it.

The authors adapt a hybrid causal discovery algorithm for astrophysical data and test it on mock catalogues, reaching about ninety percent accuracy. They then apply it to roughly half a million low-redshift galaxies from the NASA Sloan Atlas. The recovered causal graph supports a hierarchical, mass-driven picture of galaxy evolution. It also separated physical mechanisms that pure correlation analysis leaves degenerate, showing the method's added value.
arxiv-2510-01312:
Saad updates the reference tables that track how quark and lepton properties change with probing energy. Couplings and masses are not constants; they run with scale, and model builders need their values everywhere. Fresh particle data with smaller uncertainties motivated a full recomputation.

Side-by-side results use the previous and newest datasets so readers can see what shifted. Values appear for the standard model at a ladder of benchmark scales. The supersymmetric extension gets extra tables at unification scales for several parameter choices. Builders of theories beyond the standard model can test their ideas against the refreshed numbers. Smaller uncertainties in the newest release came from reduced systematic estimates. Mixing parameters run alongside the couplings in the tables. Threshold corrections from supersymmetric loops get an approximate treatment. Grand-unified scales anchor the highest benchmark column. Reference data quietly enables theory testing.
arxiv-2510-01612:
Panchumarthi and co-authors build a question-answering system that writes long, evidence-based answers to biomedical questions. Medical readers need explanations, not one-line verdicts, and the literature grows too fast to read directly. Their framework pairs retrieval with a generator fine-tuned for the biomedical domain.

Specialized embeddings and a fast index fetch candidate passages from the literature. Three re-ranking strategies compete to pick the best context before synthesis. On a standard biomedical test set, the full system beat baselines across several overlap measures. Careful retrieval plumbing, more than model size, drove the gains. BioBERT embeddings speak the vocabulary of biomedical text from the start. Re-ranking decides which evidence the generator actually sees. Parameter-efficient tuning keeps the domain adaptation affordable. Long-form answers can cite their way to trust. Clinicians need synthesis across papers, not snippets from one. Retrieval quality caps answer quality.
arxiv-2510-01912:
Ai, Cai, Zhang, and Yang rebuild hyperspectral images from compressed snapshots in this 2025 computer vision paper. Hyperspectral cameras record a full spectrum at every pixel, which makes them costly and slow. Compressive systems like CASSI capture a coded mixture instead, and software must undo the damage. Fine spectral detail is exactly what reconstruction tends to lose.

Their network, FMU, embeds a flow-matching generative prior inside a deep unfolding framework. Unfolding keeps the interpretability of an optimization algorithm, while flow matching supplies learned image knowledge. A new mean velocity loss enforces global consistency on the learned flow. The authors say this is the first use of flow matching for this reconstruction task. Experiments on simulated and real data beat existing approaches clearly. Gains were strongest for filter-based systems and real CASSI acquisitions.
arxiv-2510-02112:
Jeong and Tae lower the regularity bar for the Vlasov-Poisson equation in this 2025 analysis paper. The equation tracks a plasma or galaxy as a distribution over position and velocity, coupled to its own electric field. Well-posedness theory asks which initial data launch exactly one solution. Rougher data are more physical, but the equations may misbehave there.

The authors prove local well-posedness in Sobolev spaces with surprisingly low smoothness. In dimensions three and up, data slightly above the halfway threshold suffice. The initial distribution needs compact support in velocity, a mild physical condition. Data outside every high-integrability Lebesgue space are still allowed, a genuine extension. Velocity averaging, which smooths the density, powers the argument. The threshold improves on what scaling alone would suggest. Kinetic theorists gain room to start from realistic, irregular distributions. The result sharpens the boundary between solvable and ill-posed for a canonical model.
arxiv-2510-02212:
Zhao, Liang, Tang, Yao, and Kallus train diffusion language models to reason better and faster in this 2025 paper. Masked diffusion models generate text by unmasking tokens in parallel, but reinforcement learning for them is awkward. Their likelihoods resist the tractable forms policy optimization wants. The framework, DiFFPO, routes around that with surrogate policies.

Surrogates trained by off-policy reinforcement learning approximate the true diffusion policy with usable likelihoods. A two-stage likelihood approximation, corrected by importance sampling, sharpens that estimate further. The generalized algorithms gain sample efficiency and task performance over prior baselines. A second idea trains the sampler itself: the model learns to set its own inference threshold per prompt. That exploits the multi-token prediction these models naturally offer. Speed then adapts to difficulty instead of following a fixed schedule. Diffusion language models get both sharper reasoning and cheaper decoding from one training scheme.
arxiv-2510-02412:
Sienicki and Sienicki dispute a claimed loophole in Bell theorem reasoning. Their 2025 comment examines a model built on hierarchical arithmetics. Changing arithmetic changes how probabilities combine across levels. That formal starting point is sound, they grant. A mapping must translate probabilities between the levels. The target paper fixes that mapping by importing the Born rule. It also imports a standard quantum distance measure. Both tools come from the very theory under challenge. Quantum correlations then appear because they were built in.

The comment calls the result a hybrid framework. It mixes classical probability inside each measurement context with exotic rules across contexts. Bell theorem assumes classical probability throughout its scope. A model that drops that premise sits outside the theorem. It therefore cannot count as a genuine counterexample. Engineered agreement is not new physics. The critique defends careful premise checking in foundations debates.
arxiv-2510-02512:
Tian, Ganguly, and Macdonald retrieve ready made query variants instead of generating them. Their 2025 information retrieval paper improves query performance prediction. Predicting whether a search will succeed guides system choices. Variant queries with similar needs can sharpen that prediction. Generated variants may drift off topic or hallucinate. The team retrieves variants from a large training query set instead. A second hop through shared relevant documents widens recall. Those two hop variants track the target information need closely. Experiments ran on the TREC Deep Learning benchmarks from two years.

Retrieved variants beat the best generated variant methods clearly. Gains reached about twenty percent on neural ranking models. MonoT5 was one of the rankers showing the benefit. Real query logs make the approach practical for deployed systems. Not every target query finds good variants, they note. Coverage limits remain for rare information needs. Retrieval offers a grounded alternative to synthetic variants.
arxiv-2510-02912:
Zou and co-authors trim the visual load of multimodal language models. Such models turn images into long strings of visual tokens. Long strings make every answer slower and costlier. Pruning drops tokens, but common methods chase the flashiest spots. They keep near-duplicate tokens around a few highlights. Under heavy pruning, accuracy falls off a cliff. Their framework, HoloV, takes a wider view.

HoloV splits the token budget across spatial crops of the image. Each region keeps a fair share of its tokens. The kept set thus covers the scene as a whole. The method plugs into existing models without retraining. Tests spanned many tasks, model designs, and pruning levels. HoloV beat the best prior methods across that range. One model kept nearly all its skill after losing most tokens. Only about one token in nine survived that cut.
arxiv-2510-03512:
Tackney and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper comparing ways to fill missing outcomes in randomized clinical trials. Trials lose data when patients skip visits or drop out, and analysis must guess the gaps fairly. The team ran two simulation studies that mimic real trial data with nonlinear patterns and skewed repeated measures. They compared complete case analysis, standard imputation, predictive mean matching, and machine learning imputers such as random forests and boosted ensembles of trees.

Without treatment and covariate interplay, complete cases gave trustworthy answers in their runs. Machine learning imputers sometimes cut error in nonlinear settings but broke down in others, with biased effects or wrong standard errors. A popular matching method also misbehaved under its default settings. Filling data separately by treatment arm fixed several failures when interplay was present. Trial statisticians get a clear warning: flexible imputers need checking, not blind trust.
arxiv-2510-03612:
Jiang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper showing that AI web agents can be steered by editing a listing's picture and text. Such agents rank products and pick content for users, so a seller who biases the pick gains advantage. The attack assumes no insider access: the adversary edits only their listing, with no view of the agent's internals. Their method pairs image perturbations with wording that exploits biases baked into models by human feedback training. The team tested agents built on commercial and open vision language models.

The attack beat single channel baselines on movie and shopping tasks. Manipulation succeeded in up to seventy one percent of attempts. Detection stayed low: models hunting for manipulation caught about a quarter of cases. The results span proprietary and open agents, so the weakness looks structural rather than vendor specific. Platforms deploying shopping agents need defenses before steering becomes a marketing trick.
arxiv-2510-04112:
Pan and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on a numerical scheme for gas flows that gravitate toward themselves. Self-gravitating Euler equations model star formation and supernova remnants, but their time-dependent gravitational potential makes structure preservation hard. A good scheme should hold a polytropic equilibrium exactly and conserve total energy, in several dimensions without assuming spherical symmetry. The authors build a local discontinuous Galerkin method achieving both at high order.

Well-balancing comes from splitting the potential into equilibrium and perturbation parts, with a modified numerical flux and source discretization. For energy conservation, they rewrite the energy equation in conservative form and design the energy flux through the weak formulation. Two- and three-dimensional tests verify shock capturing, high-order accuracy, exact balance, and energy conservation. Structure-preserving methods matter because small energy leaks corrupt long astrophysical simulations.
arxiv-2510-04212:
Qiu and Yao present this 2025 arXiv paper explaining a notorious failure of low-precision transformer training with Flash Attention. Low-precision formats cut memory and boost speed, so labs push attention into BF16 and feed-forward layers even lower. Yet one long-standing configuration reliably ends in catastrophic loss explosion. The authors give the first mechanistic account of why.

Inside the attention mechanism, representations collapse toward similar low-rank forms during training. At the same time, low-precision rounding errors are biased rather than random, so they accumulate in one direction. The two effects feed each other, corrupting weight updates until training derails. To test the diagnosis, the authors make a minimal change to Flash Attention that counteracts the rounding bias. That single change stabilized the previously failing training runs. A confirmed mechanism converts folklore about low-precision instability into an actionable fix.
arxiv-2510-04412:
Takayuki Hibi and Peter Schenzel wrote this 2025 paper in algebra on how modules break into free pieces. A free resolution lists the building blocks of a module and the maps between them. Some resolutions look linear for a stretch, then jump to a higher degree, then look linear again. The size of that jump is called the gap. The pair asked whether the gap could be as large as one wishes.

They built explicit chains of free modules for four elements of a ring, with tests for when the chains are exact. Using those chains, they described the key module of a monomial curve that lies on a smooth quadric surface. The description shows the module is generated in a linear way. Yet its higher relations can have arbitrarily high degree. That example answers the opening question in the affirmative.
arxiv-2510-04512:
Fumio Nemoto and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on bike sharing systems in busy cities. Riders often find empty docks where they need a bike and full docks where they want to return one. The team modeled the system with a quantum generative model, a circuit whose time evolution mimics the data. The model learns how bike counts at each port rise and fall through the day. It also learns how ports move together.

Bike counts are naturally discrete, which suits the quantum circuit encoding well. Once trained, the model can run what if simulations of the whole network. One test added bikes early to ports with heavy demand and tracked the effect. Total rentals across the system rose in the simulation. That kind of forecast helps operators rebalance fleets before shortages bite. The core engine is a Monte Carlo simulation, so the authors see uses far beyond bikes.
arxiv-2510-04612:
Simon Boche and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a mapping system for mobile robots. A robot that moves through the world must track its own pose and build a map at the same time. Their system, OKVIS2 X, fuses camera views with motion sensors as its base senses. It can also take depth from sensors or learned estimates, laser range data, and satellite positions. One framework accepts all feeds without separate pipelines.

The map is a volume of occupied space, built from submaps that tile large areas. That design scales to runs up to nine kilometers in their tests. Alignment terms tie the estimator tightly to the submaps, which lifts both accuracy and robustness. The system can calibrate camera positions online while it runs. On a drone benchmark it took top trajectory accuracy against rival systems. The code is public, so robot teams can adopt the stack.
arxiv-2510-04812:
Grzegorz Kudra and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on disks that stick and slip while spinning on moving belts. Friction drives the motion: a disk slides and rotates on a belt, held by springs to a support. A direct current motor powers the belts, so the energy source is limited. Contact spreads over a patch, coupling the friction force and torque together. The team built a model with friction laws that avoid jumps when sliding stops.

Simulations mapped how the disks behave as settings change. The system shows stick slip motion, mixing slide and spin. Most behavior is periodic, though some cycles run long. The two disks can lock together and move in phase, or settle into counterphase motion. Maps and bifurcation diagrams chart where each regime lives. Dynamics appear in brakes, clutches, and belt drives that squeal or judder. Predicting synchronization helps engineers design chatter out, or harness it.
arxiv-2510-04912:
Ngeyen Yinkfu, Sunday Nwovu, Jonathan Kayizzi, and Angelique Uwamahoro study self-driving challenges in Rwanda in this 2025 arXiv paper. Motorcycle taxis dominate traffic in Kigali, the capital. They weave through traffic and often ignore the rules. A self-driving car there must spot motorbikes quickly and reliably to stay safe.

The team trained four well-known detection models on a custom set of 198 Kigali street images. YOLOv5 gave the best balance of accuracy and speed for live navigation. RetinaNet located bikes most precisely, but it ran too slowly for real-time use. SSD was fastest yet least accurate, while Faster R-CNN was precise but slow. The authors urge larger datasets and simpler models for poorer settings.
arxiv-2510-05112:
Lijuan Jiang and six co-authors make parallel training of giant neural networks easier to tune in this 2025 arXiv paper. Training splits a model across machines in pipeline stages. Each architecture needs its own carefully crafted schedule of micro-batches. Hand-writing those schedules is slow, and fixed presets cannot adapt to new models.

Their framework, FlexPipe, pairs a small domain-specific language with an automated scheduler. Users describe custom schedules compactly, and the scheduler explores alternatives at low search cost. The language also lets new operations enter schedules as needs change. In evaluations, FlexPipe ran up to 2.28 times faster than the popular Megatron-LM framework. It also beat a leading automated pipeline system by up to 1.49 times.
arxiv-2510-05312:
Micheli T. Moura and four co-authors test whether simulations reproduce the universe's most extreme galaxies in this 2025 arXiv paper. Massive compact galaxies, nicknamed red nuggets, formed early and barely grew afterward. Relic galaxies are their untouched survivors today. The team selected compact massive galaxies in the TNG50 simulation with criteria matching real surveys.

Simulated compacts followed the observed mass-size relation at three redshifts. Their numbers also rose toward earlier times, as observations show. Differences appeared in chemistry and motion, though. Observed relics look like outliers in velocity dispersion, while simulated ones stayed uniform across histories. Simulated compacts were all more metal-rich than typical quiet galaxies. Real relics stand out more sharply than their simulated counterparts.
arxiv-2510-05412:
Matthew Elpers shows that surgery slopes fail to identify knots far beyond the three-sphere in this 2025 arXiv paper. A characterizing slope pins down a knot: matching surgeries force the knots to be the same. Some knots, though, admit infinitely many non-characterizing slopes. Elpers generalizes that failure to arbitrary compact orientable 3-manifolds with torus boundary.

For any homotopy class in such a manifold, he produces infinitely many pairs of distinct knots representing it. The paired knots have orientation-preserving homeomorphic zero-surgeries, so surgery cannot tell them apart. Volume arguments show the knot exteriors themselves are genuinely different. The construction extends earlier counterexamples from special manifolds like the product of a sphere and a circle. Characterizing-slope hope therefore fails in full generality.
arxiv-2510-05612:
Pathak and Mankodi teach databases to predict their own query runtimes. Query optimizers pick execution plans using cost models built on static heuristics. Those guesses often miss real performance under complex, shifting workloads. Their 2025 framework replaces the guesses with machine learning on execution plan features.

The pipeline generates parameterized TPC-H queries and runs them in PostgreSQL. Over a thousand queries supply execution traces for training. Scalar, structural, and semantic features describe each plan and query. The team compares baseline regressors, a tuned XGBoost model, and an LSTM. XGBoost wins clearly, landing within ten percent of true runtime in over sixty-five percent of cases. The framework is reproducible and extensible for other database systems. Better runtime estimates mean better plans, lower latency, and steadier service levels. Tree learning on real plan features looks ready for real optimizers.
arxiv-2510-05712:
Jiang and colleagues read the ashes of the first stars in ancient survivors. Extremely metal-poor stars carry the chemical fingerprints of the universe's first supernovae. Those explosions came from Population III stars, the first generation ever formed. Their 2025 study fits the fingerprints with Bayesian inference to recover the culprits.

The team first applied NLTE corrections to the measured abundances. Those corrections shrank mismatches for odd elements like sodium and aluminum. Their framework also handles explodability and uneven model grids without bias. Three homogeneous samples from high-resolution spectroscopy fed the analysis. Fits confirm a top-heavy initial mass function for the massive first stars. They also derive a mass-energy relation for the first supernovae. Energy grows with the square of the progenitor's mass. A new sensitivity metric shows which elements steer the progenitor inference most. Abundance work thus probes early supernova physics independently.
arxiv-2510-06012:
Tschofenig and Guilbeault study how behaviors, ideas, and products spread through social networks in a 2025 paper. They focus on complex contagions, which people adopt only after several contacts have adopted them first. Simple contagions, such as easy information, need just one contact.

The authors build a causal framework that simulates the possible paths a contagion could take and ranks the links and people that matter most. Their central discovery is that complex contagion paths often work in only one direction, even on networks drawn as fully symmetric. The more social proof adoption requires, the stronger this one-way pattern becomes. Spread also tends to run from the edge of a network toward its core, which reverses standard centrality thinking. The framework explains odd patterns in a LinkedIn study of how jobs spread.
arxiv-2510-06112:
Chandrasekaran and three co-authors explain when a hard optimization problem secretly has a convex twin in a 2025 mathematics paper. Some nonconvex problems become solvable after the right transformation, a phenomenon called hidden convexity. Knowing in advance which problems enjoy the trick has been difficult.

The team introduces the Lagrangian dual section, a continuous choice of Lagrange multipliers maximizing the Lagrangian. When such a section exists, the nonconvex problem admits a natural convex reformulation. The proofs lean only on continuity and connectedness, so topology does the heavy lifting. The framework unifies results for inverse spectral problems, including quadratic programs with quadratic constraints and Stiefel manifold optimization. It also covers unbalanced Procrustes problems, a staple of shape alignment. A Lie theory angle ties the spectral cases to the Kostant convexity theorem. New algorithms find globally optimal solutions on curved spaces.
arxiv-2510-06512:
Khare and four co-authors lift per-frame detector scores into temporal property scores in a 2025 computer vision paper. Detectors like YOLO and HuBERT score local properties, like a car in a frame or anger in speech. Users ask temporal questions: did the speaker eventually sound happy, or where does a car appear until a pedestrian shows up?

The authors formalize temporal property scoring over noisy prediction sequences. Their LogSTOP function computes such scores efficiently for Linear Temporal Logic properties. Query matching pairs LogSTOP with YOLO for video objects and HuBERT for speech emotions. It beat large vision/audio language models and other temporal-logic baselines by at least sixteen percent. Ranked retrieval over video objects and actions showed similar dominance. Mean average precision rose at least nineteen percent over zero-shot baselines. Formal temporal logic still outperforms giant multimodal models at structured temporal questions.
arxiv-2510-06612:
Zibo Su, Kun Wei, Jiahua Li, Xu Yang, and Cheng Deng build talking faces that speak many languages. Their 2025 paper addresses speech-driven face animation from audio. Current systems work well in English but falter in other languages. They produce wrong mouth shapes and stiff expressions. English-heavy training data and weak cross-language transfer cause the gap.

Their framework, MuEx, uses speech sounds and mouth shapes as a shared bridge. Sounds are broken into phonemes, and mouth positions into visemes, which both act as universal units. An alignment mechanism links the two sets across languages. A mixture-of-experts design then routes each case to suitable specialist parts. The team also built a test set covering twelve languages. MuEx led on multilingual lip sync while keeping its English quality. It even generalized to languages it had never seen in training.
arxiv-2510-06712:
Fabian Rennecke and Shi Yin study an odd regime predicted inside extremely dense matter. Their 2025 paper concerns the moat regime in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons. In this regime, a meson's lowest energy sits at nonzero momentum, which is unusual. Low-energy models can describe the regime, but model artifacts can mislead.

The authors use a two-flavor quark-meson model at finite temperature and density. They propose a clean renormalization scheme that handles the momentum dependence of meson energies. Renormalization conditions matter greatly for consistent results here. Small changes in those conditions can shift conclusions about the moat. The regime's size in the phase diagram also depends critically on how quarks and mesons interact. Their message is cautionary for the field. Claims about the moat regime at zero density can be model artifacts. Careful renormalization is required before trusting effective-model predictions about dense matter.
arxiv-2510-06912:
Alexandros Vassiliades leads a team testing whether language models can build explainable machine learning pipelines on their own. Their 2025 paper prompts three leading systems, from OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek, to design training workflows. Two tasks anchor the study. One predicts driver alertness from behavior features, and the other is a multilabel problem on yeast data.

Each model wrote pipelines for four standard classifiers, from random forests to recurrent networks. The team scored the outputs on predictive quality and on explainability. Explainability was measured with SHAP, which credits each feature for its influence. Two SHAP measures mattered most, namely how faithfully the credits track the model and how few features dominate. The language models produced pipelines that matched hand-built baselines. Their explanations stayed faithful and sparse, like the human versions. The study marks a check on autonomous data science. It also flags limits that follow-up work should probe.
arxiv-2510-07312:
Motwani and co-authors present h1, a method that teaches language models to reason over much longer chains. Their 2025 paper starts from a clear weakness. Models handle short problems well but fade as steps multiply. Step-by-step supervision is costly, and prompting tricks scale poorly. The team instead builds long problems by composing short ones into dependency chains. Abundant easy data thereby becomes hard training material of any length.

Training uses reinforcement learning with rewards only for final answers. A curriculum raises the chain length automatically as the model improves. Models trained on composed grade-school math problems gained up to about double accuracy on harder contest benchmarks. Skills also transferred to unrelated reasoning gyms and long-context tests. Gains held even when many attempts were allowed, showing genuinely new solution paths. The approach offers a cheap route to long-horizon reasoning without new human-labeled data.
arxiv-2510-07512:
Nelson, Rajakumar, and Gullans find a sharp depth limit beyond which noisy quantum circuits forget everything fed into them. Their 2025 paper studies encoding information with random noisy circuits. It was known that very deep noisy circuits without resets output near-total noise, erasing all input. The open question was whether shallow circuits can preserve information by encoding it into an error-correcting codespace as they go. Simulations reveal a clean phase transition. Below a critical depth that scales inversely with the noise rate, quantum information survives the encoding.

The authors then prove this trade-off is the best any noisy circuit can achieve when encoding a constant rate of information. Random circuits, often treated as toy chaos generators, are therefore optimal noisy encoders in this precise sense. The result ties the breakdown of long-range entanglement to the encoding failure at the same threshold.
arxiv-2510-08612:
Devang Dhanuka reviews how large language models are changing teamwork in software development in a 2025 arXiv paper. The study reframes and updates earlier work with literature and case studies current as of 2025. It follows collaboration across the full software development life cycle, from planning to release. Tools examined include AI project management agents and assistants that generate code.

Evidence comes from two case studies, a team survey, industry examples, and a literature review. Dhanuka finds language models raise efficiency by automating documentation and other repetitive tasks. Communication clarity and cross-functional collaboration also benefit, according to the gathered evidence. New challenges arrive alongside: model limitations and privacy concerns head the list. The paper sets out research questions, evaluates threats to validity, and suggests future directions. Domain-specific customization, deeper tool integration, and trust and security strategies are proposed.
arxiv-2510-08712:
Zheheng Liu, Nicola Vigano, Henry Proudhon, and Wolfgang Ludwig set out the math behind topo-tomography in a 2025 arXiv paper. This X-ray method maps grain shape and crystal tilt inside materials made of many small crystals. It uses diffraction, the bending of X-rays by crystal planes, at a synchrotron light source. Turning its raw data into 3D maps of grain tilt lacked a firm theory until now.

The team derives formulas for the imaging geometry under a simple diffraction model. Grain shape, small lattice turns inside each grain, and elastic strain all enter the formulas. Small-strain and small-grain shortcuts then simplify the math a great deal. The worked images match views of a slightly warped grain volume, they show. Fourier tools on that volume reveal when tilt field recovery can work. They also give a lower bound for sampling fineness, checked in simulations.
arxiv-2510-08812:
Kim and colleagues design a planner that lets a distant spacecraft run its own science, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Deep space probes face radio delays of an hour or more, so ground teams cannot steer them live. Samples gathered in a search for life can also spoil within days. The planner must therefore decide on board which instrument to run next, under deep uncertainty about what the samples hold.

Their framework treats the problem as decision making with partial information, a standard formalism for acting under uncertainty. A Bayesian network, a compact web of linked probabilities, organizes the messy measurements inside it. Policies are computed on Earth before launch, so they can be checked thoroughly. Tested on the proposed Enceladus Orbilander life-detection suite, the planner cut sample identification errors by nearly forty percent against the mission's baseline plan, and it held up when samples arrived off schedule.
arxiv-2510-09012:
Ma and a large team improve image generators by listening to the information content of each token, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Autoregressive image models emit a picture token by token, borrowing machinery built for text. The authors observe that image tokens differ from words: each carries less information, and that information is spread unevenly across the picture. Treating all positions alike wastes effort on empty sky and starves busy detail.

Their decoding strategy adjusts the randomness of sampling, called temperature, according to the spatial entropy of the token distribution at each step. Busy regions get careful, conservative choices, while dull regions move fast. A second rule uses the same entropy signal to accept or reject drafted tokens in speculative decoding, a shortcut that guesses ahead. The combination raised quality and speed together across many models, reaching near-lossless output at a fraction of the usual acceleration cost.
arxiv-2510-09212:
Li and co-authors teach a video generator to learn from its own mistakes so it can produce endless, steady footage, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Long video generators drift because each new frame is built on their own imperfect earlier frames, while training only ever showed them clean footage. Errors compound until scenes repeat or dissolve. Most fixes patch symptoms with handcrafted tricks. This team closes the gap between training and use.

Their method, error-recycling fine-tuning, deliberately injects the model's past errors into training inputs, simulating the messy trajectories it will face when generating. The errors are collected cheaply and stored in a replay bank, then resampled to supervise new corrections. The model learns to notice and fix its own drift. The system scales clips from seconds to effectively infinite length at no extra generation cost. It accepts text, audio, and skeleton guidance, and led on three benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-09512:
Mark Jones and Jannik Schestag study conservation planning with evolutionary trees in a 2025 arXiv paper. The phylogenetic diversity of a set of species is the total branch length connecting them on their family tree. Choosing small sets with maximal diversity tells planners where scarce conservation money does the most good. Real cases add two complications: relationships may form a network rather than a tree, and a food web constrains which species can survive together.

The authors define decision problems that combine a phylogenetic network, a food web, and targets for set size and diversity. A chosen set must also stay viable, meaning enough prey species survive to support the predators. They map the parameterised complexity of these problems, asking which combinations of parameters make them efficiently solvable. For several favourable combinations they give fixed-parameter tractable algorithms, completing a dichotomy that separates the tractable cases from the rest.
arxiv-2510-09612:
Vikash Sahu, Waseem Lone, and Amit Verma develop wavelet tools tied to a special transform in a 2025 arXiv paper. The special affine Fourier transform generalises the classic frequency analysis of signals with extra parameters. Its multiresolution analysis gives a structured way to build orthonormal bases, sets of perfectly independent building blocks, for the space of finite-energy signals.

Motivated by the need to sample band-limited signals in this transform domain, the authors establish a sampling theory for it. Sampling theory states when a continuous signal can be rebuilt exactly from discrete snapshots. They construct multiresolution structures inside the transform domain that support the formation of orthonormal wavelet bases. A method for building such bases in the signal space is proposed, and the theory is demonstrated through worked examples. The authors present the framework as a foundation for advanced signal analysis in this generalised frequency setting.
arxiv-2510-10212:
Yu. Kulinich and co-authors compute the global signals of the first molecules in this 2025 arXiv paper in cosmology. In the dark ages, before the first stars, the first molecules formed: hydrogen, hydrogen deuteride, and helium hydride. Their spin and vibration lines can create faint global signals that telescopes may one day pick up.

The authors ask how primordial magnetic fields, weak fields that may date from the early universe, change that chemistry. They model how the molecules form and how their energy levels fill up when such fields are present. If the fields heat or cool the gas, the predicted signals shift. The size of the shift tells observers whether a future detection could also reveal the fields.
arxiv-2510-10312:
Ablowitz, Ramesh Gupta, Ziad H. Musslimani, and Nicholas J. Ossi derive a six-wave interaction system in this 2025 arXiv paper in nonlinear optics. Multi-wave interactions describe how light beams exchange energy in a nonlinear medium. The authors start from Maxwell's equations for the electric and polarization fields.

A space-time multi-scale asymptotic expansion then produces a hierarchy of coupled equations for the evolving fields. From that hierarchy they obtain the six-wave interaction system in several dimensions. They also study a space-time shifted reduction of the system, a simpler special case with its own dynamics. Exact reduced models of light-matter interaction feed both theory and the design of photonic devices.
arxiv-2510-10812:
William Acero, Isabel Molina, and J Miguel Marín estimate statistics for small regions in years when no census is taken, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Official statistics often lean on census microdata, which ages badly between censuses. Their procedure replaces the outdated census file with a bigger unit level survey covering the areas of interest and records useful auxiliary variables.

They also develop a mean squared error estimator that accounts for the uncertainty introduced by using the large survey in place of the census. In empirical results, their predictors clearly beat alternatives when census data are outdated. When census data are correct, the predictors stay very close to optimal. The new error estimator also corrects the bias of purely model based error estimators that ignore the survey's own uncertainty. The method targets statistics producers who must publish regional figures every year.
arxiv-2510-10912:
Xinyu Shao and eight co-authors replace the single target point in robot grounding with a heatmap, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language guided robots usually collapse spatial reasoning into discrete points, which makes them brittle to noisy perception and ambiguous wording. Their framework, RoboMAP, turns spatial targets into continuous affordance heatmaps that adapt. The dense representation carries uncertainty about where the target is, and gives downstream control policies richer information to act on.

RoboMAP surpassed the previous state of the art on a majority of grounding benchmarks, with up to a fiftyfold speed improvement. In real world manipulation it achieved an 82 percent success rate in the reported experiments. Across extensive simulated and physical tests, it stayed robust and showed strong zero shot generalization to navigation. The authors argue that carrying uncertainty explicitly, instead of committing to one point early, improves both task success and interpretability.
arxiv-2510-11012:
Sanchit Sinha, Guangzhi Xiong, and Aidong Zhang hand vision language models a reasoning scaffold built from concept trees, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These models falter at compositional reasoning: tasks that hinge on how several objects, attributes, and relations interact in an image. Prompt tricks help inconsistently, and borrowing a big language model's reasoning is costly or opaque. Their COCO-Tree method augments model outputs with neurosymbolic concept trees learned from language models, then reasons over them with a beam search like process.

The trees make the reasoning interpretable: readers can see the rationale behind a prediction. The team tested four compositionality benchmarks: Winoground, EqBench, ColorSwap, and SugarCrepe. Across seven open source vision language models of varying sizes, COCO-Tree improved compositional generalization by 5 to 10 percent over baselines in the reported experiments. Structured concepts, the authors argue, supply the linguistic discipline that raw vision models lack.
arxiv-2510-11812:
Souradeep Mukhopadhyay and seven colleagues test whether large language models truly reason or merely remember. Models ace classic logic puzzles, but those puzzles fill their training data. The team's 2025 arXiv paper introduces PHANTOM RECALL, a benchmark of twenty-five famous puzzles plus one hundred forty-nine careful edits. Each edit keeps the reasoning structure but changes surface details and the correct answer.

The researchers evaluated eleven leading models, including the GPT, Gemini, and Claude families. On untouched puzzles the models scored near perfectly. On edited ones they fell well below human performance. The failure mode is telling: models confidently recited the memorized solution even when it no longer fit, a habit the authors name phantom recall. They also over-explained simple problems. The team contributes three tools: an automated judge of logical equivalence, a taxonomy of reasoning errors, and a prompting framework built from that taxonomy to reduce the mistakes.
arxiv-2510-12312:
Delgrange, Avalos, and Röpke bring the safety guarantees of safe policy improvement into online reinforcement learning with learned world models, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Safe policy improvement aims to update a decision making policy without risking a drop in performance. Existing guarantees mostly cover offline, tabular settings, far from the deep learning agents used in practice.

The authors develop theory showing that restricting updates to a clearly defined neighborhood of the current policy ensures monotone improvement and convergence in general online settings. Their analysis ties transition and reward prediction losses to the quality of the learned representation. Building on this, they introduce DeepSPI, an on policy algorithm pairing local model losses with regularized policy updates. On the ALE-57 benchmark of Atari games, DeepSPI matched or beat strong baselines including PPO and DeepMDPs. Unusually for a deep method, it does so while keeping the theoretical guarantees that motivated the design.
arxiv-2511-00112:
Yanbing Mao, Yihao Cai, and Lui Sha introduce Real-DRL, a framework that lets a deep reinforcement learning agent learn safely at runtime on a real physical plant. Safety-critical systems cannot afford exploratory failures, yet offline training rarely matches reality. Three components interact: a learning student agent, a physics-model-based teacher, and a trigger that mediates between them.

The student uses dual self-learning and teaching-to-learn ideas with real-time safety-informed batch sampling, while the physics teacher guards safe behavior. Control readers get a design for learning in reality without surrendering safety. Runtime learning on real plants could adapt controllers to wear and drift that simulators never modeled.
arxiv-2511-00312: J-H Eschenburg, K K Santos, and R Tribuzy study equivariant embeddings, maps that place a symmetric Kählerian space inside another space while keeping its symmetries. Guided by a theorem of Cartan and Wallach on such embeddings, they describe the embeddings fully for one key case, the complex projective space. They also prove that an embedding with parallel plurimean curvature must be the standard symmetric one. The note is short and written for experts in geometry.
arxiv-2511-00812:
Shashank Nag and a large team present LL-ViT, a vision transformer redesigned to run on low power edge hardware such as FPGA chips. Transformers lead on vision tasks, but their size, memory use, and energy needs make small devices a poor fit.

The design swaps the transformer's channel mixer, where most weights and computation sit, for neurons built from lookup tables that are learned directly during training. A custom FPGA accelerator runs the result. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, accuracy stays close to the baseline transformer, while over sixty percent of the weights and half the multiplications disappear. The system also improves energy efficiency and latency over a quantized transformer accelerator at a modest power budget.
arxiv-2511-01112:
Luana Passos-Reis and colleagues model how cosmic rays are accelerated in the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068. That the IceCube observatory has identified as a likely neutrino source despite no matching gamma ray signal. The missing gamma rays suggest strong absorption, plus a hadronic component and efficient particle acceleration near the central black hole.

Their one zone model places the action in the coronal accretion flow, where turbulence driven magnetic reconnection accelerates protons and electrons. Photon fields in the corona serve as targets for proton interactions, and pair production attenuates the gamma rays. Contrary to some recent studies, they find the extreme energies needed come mainly from first order Fermi acceleration inside the turbulent reconnection layers of a large scale current sheet.
arxiv-2511-20112:
Amano, Ohshiro, Suzuki, Fukushima, and Yamaguchi map plasma conditions across a supernova remnant. Their 2025 paper uses the Reflection Grating Spectrometer aboard XMM-Newton. The target, DEM L71, is a fairly wide remnant. High-resolution X-ray spectra reveal individual emission lines. Line ratios diagnose temperature and plasma processes region by region.

The grating's wide dispersion spread lines across the detector. That spread let the team reconstruct spatial line maps. Oxygen lines came mostly from surrounding interstellar gas. Iron emission traced the star's ejected debris instead. Images blurred along that spread direction visibly. Expansion of gas and ejecta explains that blur. Some regions showed oddly lopsided oxygen line ratios. Plain shock-heated plasma models cannot explain those ratios. Resonance scattering can account for the enhancement. Charge exchange offers another plausible contributor there. The ratios grew alongside forbidden line brightness.
arxiv-2511-20212:
Wang, Chen, Sun, and Zhang settle when scoring a quantum optimizer is itself hard. Their 2025 paper analyzes QAOA expectation computation at fixed rounds. QAOA is a leading quantum method for hard puzzles. Judging its expected score guides its use. For general problems that judgment was murky.

For Max-Cut on general graphs, exact scoring is NP-hard. That holds for any fixed round count of two or more. Even rough additive approximations stay NP-hard too. The error tolerance shrinks exponentially yet hardness persists. A dynamic programming algorithm offers the other side. It exploits tree decompositions of the input graph. When local treewidth grows only logarithmically, scoring becomes fast. Polynomial-time exact evaluation follows in that regime. The framework extends beyond Max-Cut to binary problems generally. Tests ran up to three rounds on structured graphs. Locality-matched classical baselines framed the cut ratios.
arxiv-2511-20312:
Beiser, Martinelli, Gerstner, and Brea steal a neural network's weights using only its answers. Their 2025 paper reverse-engineers networks from input-output queries. A student network trains to mimic a hidden teacher. Enough probing should reveal the teacher's parameters. Standard training data often fails as query sets though.

Big teachers have more weights than available data points. Students then overfit queries instead of matching weights. Classic image tricks like rotation and noise help little. The team designed augmentations aimed at hidden layers. Their queries excite richer internal representations deliberately. Biased-noise augmentation aligned student and teacher weights excellently. Previously unrecoverable teachers on MNIST became identifiable. The method scales far beyond earlier limits. Networks with one hundred times more parameters than data were recovered. The augmented set grew to thirty-five times the original size. Scaling tests stopped at 512 hidden neurons.
arxiv-2511-20412:
Wang, Slud, and Ma trace how genes might cause brain disorders through brain wiring. Their 2025 paper builds a new mediation model for imaging genetics. Disorders like nicotine dependence run in families and involve many genes. Genes likely act by changing brain structure and function first. Mediation analysis makes that chain of influence precise. Thousands of genes and brain features overwhelm older versions.

Their model handles many exposures and many mediators jointly. Both sides compress into low-dimensional summary scores. Those summaries are chosen to maximize the mediation effect. Sparsity in the loadings keeps the summaries easy to read. An alternating algorithm with block updates solves the fitting problem. Simulations beat rival methods across signal and noise settings. Applied to UK Biobank data, the method linked genes to smoking. Specific genes affected nicotine dependence via wiring changes in the brain. Particular brain regions carried those indirect effects.
arxiv-2511-20612:
Kim and Dean rebuild whole flow fields from a sparse scatter of sensors. Their 2025 paper introduces Stochastic NODE-DMD for system identification. Wind fields and ocean currents evolve continuously and resist modeling. Classic dynamic mode decomposition assumes dense, clean data. Noise, sparsity, and nonlinearity break it in practice.

Their method recasts decomposition as a generative model. A neural implicit field allows reconstruction at any coordinate. A stochastic neural ODE adds the nonlinear leftovers to linear modes. Uncertainty travels with the predictions, properly quantified. Four benchmarks tested the approach against baselines. Only ten percent observation density was allowed in training. Reconstruction accuracy beat the baseline under that sparsity. Learned modes and eigenvalues matched ground truth structure. Long rollouts kept coherent geometry and phase. Training on many runs learned a spread of dynamics, not one average. Balloon and drone navigation in wind are target uses.
arxiv-2511-20812:
Chiara Fusar Bassini and colleagues test in 2025 whether automated price caps in US electricity markets deter market power, or merely look strict. Automated mitigation procedures screen bids in real time and penalise abusive prices, but only switch on when a structural index like congestion crosses a cutoff. The authors exploit that quirk with a regression discontinuity design on 2019 bid data from the New England and New York markets.

The deterrence is real but narrow. Around 30 to 40 percent of bidders cut their bids when screening activates. The median cut is 4 to 5 dollars per megawatt-hour in New England and 9 to 10 in New York. Yet the market-wide effect, a dip of 1 to 2 dollars, is not detectable, suggesting thresholds set in the early 2000s, never recalibrated, are too lax. Their merit-order simulation prices tighter thresholds at 350,000 to 980,000 dollars of buyer surplus per mitigated hour. Such hours number fewer than 33 a year.
arxiv-2511-20912:
Dongxing He, Arianna Formenti, Spencer Gessner, and Michael Peskin simplify in 2025 the physics of beamstrahlung, the hard radiation electrons and positrons emit when dense bunches collide. At future 10 TeV colliders, bunches of a billion to ten billion particles will pass through each other's intense fields. Beamstrahlung sets the energy spectrum of the most energetic particles and seeds every other quantum process, so collider designers need it in fast, usable form.

The simplification appears when the quantum parameter Upsilon grows large. It is of order 1 for colliders below 1 TeV, but reaches roughly a thousand at 10 TeV. In that limit, the electron and photon spectra collapse onto universal functions, independent of machine details. The authors supply analytical approximations to those functions, ready for general beam-beam studies. The work backs wakefield collider designs now being drawn up for the next energy frontier.
arxiv-2511-21012:
Hyunwook Jheonn and colleagues sharpen in 2025 the sorting of two easily confused star types: young stellar objects, stars still forming, and asymptotic giant branch stars, dying suns swollen and dusty. Both glow similarly in infrared light, thanks to comparable temperatures and dust shells, so catalogues contaminate each other. Their Double Filter Model adds a second sieve beyond colours and magnitudes: light curves, since the two classes vary by different mechanisms.

The model was validated on Taurus young stars and spectroscopically confirmed giant branch stars, and it caught objects that infrared-only classification had mislabelled. The team then applied it to the SPICY catalogue, the largest young-star candidate list, with nearly 120,000 sources in the inner galactic plane, to flag hidden giant-branch contaminants for follow-up spectroscopy. Earlier machine-learning efforts topped out near 90 percent accuracy in the overlap regions; the time-domain filter aims to clean what photometry cannot.
arxiv-2511-21112:
Swathi Shetty, Sayinath Udupa N. V., and B. R. Rakshith study in 2025 coalitions in graphs, in domination theory. A dominating set is a set of vertices so placed that every outside vertex touches one of them. A coalition is a pair of disjoint sets that each fail to dominate alone but dominate together when united. A coalition partition splits the vertices into such partnering sets; the coalition graph records the partnerships.

Earlier work proved every graph can appear as the coalition graph of some larger graph, but asked whether a smaller host would do. The authors answer yes, constructing a small host whose coalition graph reproduces a given graph. They also take up the coalition count, the most distinct coalitions in a partition, defined recently by Haynes and colleagues. They characterise graphs whose coalition count equals one, and derive properties of the count under conditions on the coalition number.
arxiv-2511-21312:
Martin Jacquet, Marvin Harms, and Kostas Alexis give flying robots a learned sense of nearby space in a 2025 robotics paper. Their drones navigate unknown, cluttered places without a prebuilt map, using only onboard range sensing. Two cascaded neural networks compress a single depth image into a compact code. They then expand it into a signed distance function, a field stating how far each point is from the nearest surface.

Jacquet and his coauthors embed that distance field as an explicit safety constraint inside a nonlinear model predictive controller, which plans thrust and attitude commands while tracking a target velocity. They verify the controller's recursive feasibility and stability under fixed observations. Closed-loop tests beat two leading local navigation methods, tolerated drifting odometry, and real flights in forests showed the system dodging trees and clutter against an adversarial reference velocity pushing it toward trouble.
arxiv-2511-21512:
Sara Ellison and Leonardo Ferreira weigh the stars that galaxy mergers actually build, in the fourth paper of a series, in 2025. Mergers are known to ignite central bursts of star formation, which should pile new stellar mass into galactic cores, but direct measurements of that burst mass fraction are rare. The authors assemble about 14,000 post-coalescence galaxies, systems whose merger starbursts have just finished, and compare their central masses against carefully matched non-merging controls.

Ellison and Ferreira find burst mass fractions of 10 to 20 percent, measured both in a fixed central aperture and in the galactic bulge. For 61 nearby systems with MaNGA integral-field data, the central excess runs 15 to 20 percent. Surprisingly, a 15 percent excess persists out to about 7 kiloparsecs, far wider than the compact growth earlier studies inferred. Theirs is the first such measurement made directly from stellar mass, independent of population modeling or light-profile fitting.
arxiv-2511-21612:
Shahir Abdullah and Syed Rohit Zaman argue that cloud databases scale in the wrong direction, in 2025. Providers offer a binary choice: scale out by adding nodes, or scale up by fattening each node. Reality is joint: performance and cost emerge from node count interacting with per-node CPU, memory, bandwidth, and storage speed. One-dimensional reactions overshoot load spikes or oscillate between poor states.

Their Scaling Plane maps every configuration as a point: node count on one axis, per-node resources on the other, with surfaces for latency, throughput, overhead, and cost. Analysis and experiments show optimal scaling paths often run diagonally, adjusting both dimensions at once. Their DiagonalScale algorithm searches horizontal, vertical, and diagonal moves for the best configuration under service-level constraints. Tests on synthetic surfaces and distributed SQL and key-value systems show lower tail latency, lower cost, and far better stability, with monotone convergence guaranteed.
arxiv-2511-21812:
Vandersnickt and colleagues report evidence for a magnetic field buried inside HD 192575, a hot star about twelve times the Sun's mass that pulses in brightness. They studied 1,951 days of light-curve data from the TESS space telescope, focusing on one pulsing pattern split into nine closely spaced frequencies. Explaining all nine at once is the key test.

Rotation alone, including the Coriolis effect from the star's roughly 5.3 day spin period near its core, could not reproduce the nine frequencies and their relative strengths. Adding a tilted internal magnetic field did work, with a peak strength near 24 kilogauss in the successful model. The authors present this as the first such modelled detection inside an evolved star of this type, a future supernova. It matters because hidden fields can move angular momentum and mix material inside stars.
arxiv-2511-22012:
Parekh, Gao, and Jaiman, engineers, build a stand-in for fluid-structure simulations of inverted elastic foils, flexible panels clamped at the trailing edge that flap in a flowing fluid like fluttering leaves. Such self-sustained flapping can harvest energy from currents, but high-fidelity simulations are too slow to search wide design spaces, so a trustworthy surrogate has real practical value for energy-harvesting devices.

The network treats mesh nodes and elements together as a hypergraph. Their rotation-equivariant hypergraph neural network compresses the foil's mesh motion with proper orthogonal decomposition and evolves the flow field on the mesh itself. It is trained on finite-element simulation data across a range of mass ratios. Over thousands of time steps the surrogate predicts tip displacement and force coefficients with errors below 1.5 percent, reproduces the vortex-shedding frequencies, and matches energy-transfer metrics within 3 percent of the simulations.
arxiv-2511-22312:
Praharaj and Kasundra tackle a trust problem with generative AI classifiers used for content safety. Models like LLaMA Guard label unsafe content and its categories, but they output words, not probabilities. Without class probabilities, moderators cannot judge confidence, set flexible thresholds, or study errors closely. That gap limits fine-grained error analysis for the teams who run these systems.

The team proposes three ways to recover probabilities from the model's token scores, called logits. The three are conditional, joint, and marginal probability estimates over the label tokens. They test the methods on a synthetic, carefully annotated dataset across several instruction-tuned models. Using logits clearly improves how readable and trustworthy the classifiers are. The marginal method, which adds up probability across many token paths, gives the most robust and accurate confidence scores. It also delivers the best overall classification scores of the methods tried.
arxiv-2511-22412:
Nam studies how chiral symmetry, a symmetry between left- and right-handed quarks, is restored in hot, dense quark matter. Inside the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, an effective theory of quarks, heating or compressing matter melts the quark condensate and shrinks the dynamical quark mass toward zero. Nam proposes a diagnostic built from quantum information: a chirality entanglement entropy measuring how mixed the two sectors are.

The entropy is computed from the lesser Green's function, which tracks how quarks are distributed, projected onto the left-handed sector. It rises steadily with temperature and chemical potential. It approaches its maximum exactly as the dynamical mass vanishes. This mirrors the model's phase structure: a second-order transition in the chiral limit and a smooth crossover for realistic quark masses. Its critical exponent comes out near one, supporting the entropy as an information-based probe linking mass generation to entanglement.
arxiv-2511-22612:
Sousa, Lima, and Trojahn teach a language model to align ontologies using training data the model itself helped create. Ontology matching finds correspondences between concepts of two knowledge graphs with schemas, a prerequisite for merging them. Asking a language model to match is promising but starved of examples, since reference alignments are scarce. Their pipeline shrinks each ontology to submodules, builds prompts from them, and uses an LLM-based generator to synthesise submodule pairs with reference alignments for fine-tuning.

Evaluated on five OAEI complex track datasets, Conference, Geolink, Enslaved, Taxon, and Hydrography, the fine-tuned model beat its base version in zero-shot matching. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improved one-to-one alignments, and cross-validation fine-tuning raised precision on complex ones. Limits remain: recall was limited, and complex many-to-many correspondences performed poorly. Richer synthetic data and better search-space reduction are the routes forward.
arxiv-2512-00012:
Andrei Enea introduces Painting with Code, an editor that eases children from block coding to real text code. The jump from dragging blocks to typing syntax is a known hurdle in school computer science, especially for children aged eight to ten. Many learners stall exactly at that transition.

The web-based editor uses authentic JavaScript syntax, but wraps it in a simple drawing library. Each line of code gives immediate artistic feedback on screen. Learning syntax through drawing keeps motivation high while the code stays real. A simplified, function-based drawing library keeps the first steps gentle while the syntax itself stays fully authentic.
arxiv-2512-00312:
After a penalty in rugby union, a team must choose: kick at goal for points, or kick to touch and chase a try. Kenny Watts and Jonathan Pipping build an expected points framework for that decision in 2025. The value of each option depends on field location and game context.

Expected points models convert a game situation into the points a team can expect from it on average. Comparing the two kicks on that scale gives coaches a principled guide instead of habit or gut feeling. The framework is a neat example of sports analytics turning a sideline judgment call into a measurable trade-off.
arxiv-2512-00412:
Large reasoning models think out loud in chains of thought, which creates new safety risks. Jiawei Chen and co-authors red-team such models in 2025, probing attacks like chain-of-thought hijacking and prompt-induced inefficiency. Existing evaluation methods do not fully capture these failure modes.

Explicit reasoning improves transparency and logical consistency, but the visible trace is also an attack surface. Red teaming means attacking the models deliberately to find weaknesses before bad actors do. The study helps safety teams design evaluations matched to how reasoning models actually fail, rather than borrowing tests built for older chatbots. Prompt-induced inefficiencies waste the very reasoning the models are valued for. Hijacking a chain of thought means steering the reasoning, not just the answer.
arxiv-2512-00712:
Zhuohua Liu, Kaiqi Huang, Qinxin Mei, Yuanqi Hu, and Wei Xing wrote a 2025 paper on tuning analog circuits. Designers must search for settings that make a circuit meet its goals. Most search tools treat the task as a black box over smooth functions, with no use of physics.

Yet device physics shapes circuit behavior into known families, like exponential device laws and rational transfer functions. Standard Gaussian process surrogates assume smooth, steady behavior and can misfit sharply nonlinear circuits when only fifty to one hundred tests are affordable. The authors exploit that family structure instead. Better fits at small sample sizes could cut costly design trials.
arxiv-2512-00812:
Yijia Fan, Jusheng Zhang, Kaitong Cai, Jing Yang, and Keze Wang tackle multi-label classification in a 2025 paper. In that task, one item can carry several labels at once, like a photo tagged with many objects. The task suffers from label imbalance, fake correlations, and shifts between datasets, which hurt rare labels most.

Their Causal Cooperative Game framework treats classification as teamwork among players. It mixes causal discovery, a counterfactual curiosity reward, and a causal invariance loss that favors features stable across settings. It also boosts rare labels on purpose. The mix aims for labels that stay right when conditions change.
arxiv-2512-00912:
Abdelghafour Halimi and four coauthors present ForamDeepSlice in a 2025 paper on tiny fossils and deep learning. Foraminifera are small shelled organisms whose fossils help date rocks and read past oceans. Naming their species from scans is slow, expert work.

Their framework classifies twelve foraminifera species from two-dimensional slices of three-dimensional micro-CT scans. The team curated a careful dataset from dozens of scanned specimens across many species. They kept the twelve species with enough examples for robust learning. Automating this naming could speed up geology and climate studies that rely on these fossils.
arxiv-2512-01112:
Tarun Chitra gives the first formal study of autodeleveraging in a 2025 paper. Autodeleveraging is a last-resort mechanism on perpetual futures exchanges, the main venues in crypto derivatives. When losses overwhelm the system and normal liquidations fail to preserve solvency, the exchange forcibly cuts winning positions to share the loss.

Despite the huge volume perpetual futures trade, no formal model of this mechanism existed. Chitra provides the first one, studying what outcomes are impossible and how the mechanism can be improved. A formal model lets exchanges and regulators judge whether their last-resort rules are fair and stable.
arxiv-2512-01412:
Ziqian Wang, Yuxiao Cheng, and Jinli Suo build a time-series model that can explain itself. Most explain tools just mark which points mattered. They miss big traits like trends, cycles, and sharp shifts in regime. Those traits are what humans look for in long data runs.

The new model pulls out clear causal patterns from the data. Each pattern is a named shape, like a trend or a cycle. Users can see why a forecast was made in those terms. Clear cause-based tales build trust for use in health, energy, and finance forecasts.
arxiv-2512-01712:
Aday Cardenas and co-authors show zero-point motion shapes high-harmonic spectra in solids. Reading those spectra often needs very short dephasing times. Those times are far shorter than scattering physics would suggest. That mismatch has long been a puzzle in the field.

The team shows phonon zero-point fluctuations do the job. They suppress long-range electronic coherence on their own. Clean spectra then arise with no ad-hoc decay terms. A physical cause for the decay firms up how harmonic spectra are used to probe solids. Solids from silicon to layered crystals all show the effect, so a phonon cause would unify spectra that now each need bespoke fixes.
arxiv-2512-01912:
The lonely runner conjecture is a puzzle from 1967 about runners on a circular track, each moving at a constant, different speed. It claims every runner eventually gets a clear gap from all the others. Matthieu Rosenfeld's 2025 paper proves the claim holds when there are nine runners.

The conjecture, first stated by Jörg Wills, is a known open problem in combinatorial number theory with several equivalent forms. Rosenfeld's proof sharpens the method he previously used to settle the eight-runner case, adding a couple of key improvements. Each new case brings the full conjecture, still unproven in general, a step closer.
arxiv-2512-02112:
When a system is driven across a phase transition, defects form in patterns predicted by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, a universal rule born in cosmology and condensed matter alike. Jan Balewski and a large team report in 2025 an anomaly in the counting statistics of those defects.

Their experiments used long one-dimensional chains of Rydberg atoms, cooled and driven slowly across a continuous transition. Counting defects event by event, rather than just on average, revealed behavior the standard picture did not predict. Anomalies like this matter because Kibble-Zurek scaling is used to benchmark quantum simulators and to reason about the early universe.
arxiv-2512-02312:
Dating the branches of the tree of life from DNA relies on fossil ages, and those ages are uncertain. Greg Ellison and Liang Liu present in 2025 a faster method for estimating node ages that accounts for fossil calibration uncertainty without the heavy cost of Bayesian relaxed-clock analyses.

Bayesian methods are principled but must re-evaluate the full phylogenetic likelihood again and again, which becomes crushing on large genomic datasets. Their adjusted pairwise likelihood approach approximates that work far more cheaply while staying accurate. Faster divergence dating opens evolutionary timelines to the genome-scale datasets now common in biology.
arxiv-2512-02412:
Arnav Burudgunte, Paul Valiant, and Hongao Wang, based at Purdue, work on a puzzle about rebuilding lost data. A hidden string of zeros and ones passes through a channel that deletes each bit at random. Each pass gives only a partial copy, called a trace, and the task is to rebuild the string.

For the circular form of the puzzle, the best known upper and lower bounds sit far apart. That gap is huge, described as exponential in size. The authors narrow it with new bounds, which helps show how many traces recovery truly needs. Sharper bounds tell us how much loss a string can take and still be rebuilt whole.
arxiv-2512-02512:
Aditya Chaudhary, Prachet Dev Singh, and Ankit Jha work on making small or blurry images sharp. Single image super resolution asks a model to guess fine detail that the input lacks. Their method, ViT-SR, builds on a Vision Transformer, a model that reads an image in patches.

Training runs in two stages, as the title notes. First the model learns by colorizing images, a self taught task that builds rich visual features. Then a residual upsampling stage lifts those features to a larger, sharper picture. Two stage training of this kind aims for better detail without far more data. Sharp large prints from small files would help phones, drones, and old film scans alike.
arxiv-2512-03112:
Fair credit for each input is a core goal in explainable AI. Jialai She studies Shapley values, a top method for that task, in this 2025 work. The classic method assumes payoffs add up in a simple way, which real data often break.

Heavy tails, linked features, and odd loss scales can twist the credit a feature gets. She offers a sparse, order-based form of Shapley regression for non-linear cases. Better credit scores for features help users see why a model made a call. That clarity matters in health, lending, and other high-stakes uses. Sparse results are easier to read, since only a few features earn large credit.
arxiv-2512-03312:
Proteins work by changing shape, not by sitting still. Daniel Richman, Jessica Karaguesian, Carl-Mikael Suomivuori, and Ron Dror study those shapes in this 2025 work. The spread of shapes a molecule takes is far harder to find than one folded structure.

Diffusion models can generate molecule shapes, but hidden parts of the landscape may stay unseen. The authors unlock those hidden conformations at inference time, without retraining. Fuller shape maps help explain how proteins function and fail. They may also guide drug design against flexible targets. Inference-time tricks avoid costly retraining each time a new target protein is studied.
arxiv-2512-03712:
